NeurIPS 2024Constrained bilevel optimization

A Primal-Dual-Assisted Penalty Approach to Bilevel Optimization with Coupled Constraints

Liuyuan Jiang, Quan Xiao, Victor M. Tenorio, Fernando Real-Rojas, Antonio G. Marques, Tianyi Chen

Read the paper ↗Code ↗Cite
On this page
SummaryMethodAnalysisIllustrationResultsCitation

Summary

Coupled constraints make the lower-level feasible set depend on the outer variable. This changes the derivative of the lower-level value and can make joint feasibility projections expensive. BLOCC addresses both effects with a primal-dual penalty formulation: constraint multipliers enter the value gradient, and first-order updates use projections onto separate domains. The paper establishes finite-time convergence and evaluates the method on constrained SVM training and transportation network design.

  • In Figure 1, for a positive upper variable x, the multiplier-weighted constraint derivative changes the objective-only derivative −4x into the correct value gradient 2x. Lemma 2 · Figure 1
  • BLOCC uses first-order primal-dual subproblem solves and separate-domain projections. Including the inner solves, total iteration complexity is O~(ε−5/2)\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\varepsilon^{-5/2})O(ε−5/2) in the general regime and O~(ε−3/2)\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\varepsilon^{-3/2})O(ε−3/2) in the affine-in-y regime, where ε\varepsilonε is the target squared generalized-gradient tolerance. Theorems 2–4
  • On diabetes, Table 2 reports similar test accuracy for BLOCC and LV-HBA, with lower mean runtime for BLOCC under the reported stopping rule. Table 2

Bilevel optimization on a moving feasible set

Coupled lower-level constraints

A transportation operator chooses link capacities, while passengers choose routes subject to those capacities. In the SVM application, hyperparameters bound the margin violations permitted during model fitting. Both problems have lower-level constraints that depend on the outer variable.

The boundary contributes to the derivative

The derivative of the minimum value v(x)v(x)v(x) depends on how g changes and on how the feasible boundary moves. Omitting the second contribution can reverse the gradient, as Figure 1 demonstrates. The active constraints contribute through their optimal multipliers μg∗(x)\mu_g^*(x)μg∗​(x).

A primal-dual penalty formulation

BLOCC penalizes the gap between g(x, y) and v(x)v(x)v(x) and represents the coupled inequalities with a Lagrangian term. This gives two saddle-point problems whose primal-dual solutions determine the outer gradient. The resulting algorithm uses first-order derivatives and projections onto separate domains, avoiding a joint projection onto the coupled feasible set.

Constrained response. Figure 1 uses g(x,y)=(y−2x)2g(x,y)=(y-2x)^2g(x,y)=(y−2x)2 and gc(x,y)g^c(x,y)gc(x,y) = 3x − y. For x > 0, the constraint y≥3xy\geq3xy≥3x is active, giving yg∗(x)=3xy_g^*(x)=3xyg∗​(x)=3x and v(x)=x2v(x)=x^2v(x)=x2.

Objective derivative. Evaluating the partial derivative ∇xg\nabla_x g∇x​g at the constrained response gives −4x. The true derivative of v(x)v(x)v(x) is 2x, so the objective term alone has the opposite sign.

Multiplier correction. The optimal multiplier is μg∗(x)=2x\mu_g^*(x)=2xμg∗​(x)=2x. Multiplying it by the constraint derivative contributes 6x, restoring the value gradient: −4x + 6x = 2x.

Two saddle-point solves per outer update

The original lower-level saddle problem. Approximate yg∗(x)y_g^*(x)yg∗​(x) and μg∗(x)\mu_g^*(x)μg∗​(x) to estimate the gradient of v(x)v(x)v(x), including the contribution from gc(x,y)g^c(x,y)gc(x,y).

The penalized saddle problem. Approximate yF∗(x)y_F^*(x)yF∗​(x) and μF∗(x)\mu_F^*(x)μF∗​(x) for the objective that combines f, the lower-level value-gap penalty, and the constraint Lagrangian.

The projected outer update. Combine the two primal-dual responses into the gradient estimate in Equation 13, then update x with a projection onto X. Inner updates project onto Y and the nonnegative multiplier domain.

Lower-level value gaps control response error

Lemma 1 bounds the squared distance to yg∗(x)y_g^*(x)yg∗​(x) by the gap g(x, y) − v(x)v(x)v(x) for feasible y. The penalty therefore links the single-level formulation to lower-level optimality. Theorem 1 quantifies this approximation when γ\gammaγ is chosen for the target response error.

Lemma 2

The lower-level value has a constraint-sensitive gradient

Under Assumptions 1–4 and bounded optimal multipliers, v(x)v(x)v(x) is smooth. Its gradient includes both the partial derivative of g and the multiplier-weighted partial derivative of g^c. The boundary term is what restores the correct derivative in Figure 1.

Theorems 1–4

Approximation and finite-time convergence

Theorem 1 controls the squared distance from the penalized response to yg∗(x)y_g^*(x)yg∗​(x). The outer criterion is an averaged squared generalized-gradient norm for FγF_\gammaFγ​. Including the two inner saddle-point solves, the general analysis gives O~(ε−5/2)\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\varepsilon^{-5/2})O(ε−5/2) total iterations under Assumptions 1–5. For affine-in-y constraints, an unconstrained lower domain, and the singular-value conditions in Theorem 4, the inner solver converges linearly and total complexity is O~(ε−3/2)\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\varepsilon^{-3/2})O(ε−3/2). The Õ notation suppresses logarithmic factors.

Theorems 1–4 in the paper ↗

Quadratic growth survives the coupled constraints

Strong convexity of g and convexity of the lower constraints yield the value-gap bound in Lemma 1. This supplies the lower-level error measure for the penalty reformulation.

The gradient requires two primal-dual responses

The response of the original lower problem determines ∇v(x)\nabla v(x)∇v(x). The response of the penalized problem determines the other terms in ∇Fγ(x)\nabla F_\gamma(x)∇Fγ​(x). Algorithm 1 approximates both before taking the outer step.

Inner accuracy enters the outer convergence bound

Theorem 2 separates outer progress from the error of the two saddle-point solves. Both inner error terms are multiplied by γ\gammaγ², so the subproblem tolerances must tighten as the penalty grows. Theorems 3–4 include these solves in the total complexity.

Assumptions behind the analysis

Assumptions 1–4 impose Lipschitz regularity, strong convexity of g in y, convexity of g^c in y, nonempty closed convex domains, lower-level feasibility, and linear independence of active constraint gradients in y (LICQ). Lemmas 2–3 also use bounded optimal multipliers. A sufficiently large γ\gammaγ preserves strong convexity of the penalized inner objective. The general inner-solver analysis in Theorem 3 additionally uses Assumption 5 on dual curvature near the optimum. Theorem 4 treats constraints affine in y with Y equal to the full lower-variable Euclidean space and uniformly bounded, positive singular values of the constraint matrix. The outer objective can be nonconvex.

Section 3 · Value-function derivative and convergence in the paper

Further details

Why are two primal-dual problems solved?

The original lower-level problem provides yg∗(x)y_g^*(x)yg∗​(x), μg∗(x)\mu_g^*(x)μg∗​(x), and the value gradient. The penalized problem provides yF∗(x)y_F^*(x)yF∗​(x) and μF∗(x)\mu_F^*(x)μF∗​(x). Their contributions appear together in Equation 9, which Algorithm 1 estimates before updating x.

Which projection does the formulation remove?

BLOCC avoids projecting the pair (x, y) onto the coupled feasible set. It retains projections onto the separate domains X and Y and onto the nonnegative multiplier domain.

What is the convergence target?

The analysis bounds the averaged squared generalized-gradient criterion of FγF_\gammaFγ​. A separate approximation result controls the squared distance from the penalized lower response to yg∗(x)y_g^*(x)yg∗​(x). The total complexity includes the inner work required to estimate both primal-dual responses.

Related projects

Smoothness of the Penalty Formulation for Bilevel Optimization later sharpens the curvature analysis of this framework. Efficient Penalty-Based Bilevel Methods extends that analysis and develops updates based on a flatness condition.

Transportation network design at three scales

The network experiments choose link capacities while accounting for passenger responses. Table 3 compares 3- and 9-node synthetic networks with a 26-node Seville instance containing 49,216 variables and 13,336 constraints. With γ\gammaγ = 4 and step size 1.6 × 10⁻⁴, BLOCC records runtime 6.70 × 10⁴ seconds and operator utility 138.78 on the Seville instance. LV-HBA does not reach convergence within the 24-hour limit on the 9-node or Seville instances. The transportation comparison uses LV-HBA as the baseline.

Result

On diabetes, BLOCC and LV-HBA have similar mean test accuracy, both with a reported standard deviation of 0.039. On fourclass, their means are 0.761 and 0.748. GAM has lower mean accuracy in both datasets.

Outer progress and inner solution accuracy

The complexity bounds combine projected outer updates with the work needed to solve both primal-dual subproblems. The target is the averaged squared generalized-gradient criterion for FγF_\gammaFγ​, together with the lower-level response approximation specified in Equation 4.
